articles.snippet: Hackers linked to Russia's FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has revealed.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — Hackers linked to Russia’s FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has revealed.
Using an advanced suite of tools that the researchers dubbed Cereal, a pun on the technology of serialization, emails going through Romanian government servers were scanned for a relation to NATO and the European Union. If this was discovered, the malicious software would create a copy for its Russian spymasters.
In particular, one component, CerealBox, targeted messages involving NATO and EU institutional addresses, the cybersecurity form ESET said. The module selected emails with Word or PDF attachments using predefined filters, then compressed and encrypted copies for later retrieval by the attackers.
The hack was discovered by the Bratislava-based company and made public on Nov. 10. ESET had first discovered the tool being used against Kazakhstan in November 2025, and found the infiltration of Romania’s Microsoft Exchange servers a month later.
In a blog post and press release, the company attributed the attack to the known hacking group Turla, which it said was generally considered to be affiliated with Russia’s FSB, the country’s domestic intelligence agency. Turla has also been involved in attacks against high-profile Ukrainian targets, and the researchers said 70% of countries the group targeted were post-Soviet or post-communist states in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The APT – a term designating an “Advanced Persistent Threat,” or known hacking group – primarily attacks government institutions.
ESET attributed the toolset to Turla with high confidence, citing the simultaneous use of another component publicly linked to the group and conceptual similarities to older Turla malware.
The researchers also noted a surge in activity in Kazakhstan on Jan. 15, 2026, the day after Old New Year, an informal holiday observed in Russia and some neighboring countries. “While malware does not celebrate holidays, its operators do,” the company wrote.
Romanian servers were compromised on Dec. 23, 2025, ESET researchers said; roughly a month after the cybersecurity firm first detected the same malicious code on the server of a Kazakh government agency. That discovery was the first time this tool had been seen, which the researchers described as “a previously undocumented toolset: a collection of modular .NET malware designed to run on Microsoft Exchange servers, receive commands, execute them in memory, map the compromised organization, and collect selected email messages.”
The tool was unusual for its “combination of novel techniques requiring deep knowledge of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods,” ESET wrote.
The tool was designed to be especially stealthy, meant to allow it to spy undetected at length. While malware commonly communicates with an external command-and-control server, which can lead to detection and help cybersecurity professionals trace the origin, Cereal used the target organization’s own Microsoft servers as its infrastructure.
Romania is an eastern flank member of NATO and has faced physical and digital spillover of the confrontation between Russia and the West, particularly since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Airspace violations, drone shootdowns and even the strike of commercial vessels in its exclusive economic zone have been among the consequences.
The country has also been targeted by cyber warfare. In May 2025, another known Russian APT actor attacked arms makers involved in supporting Ukraine, including those located in Romania; and just months after the war broke out, government websites were hit by a crude distributed denial-of-service attack, making Romanian public-authority and financial-sector websites unavailable for several hours.

articles.title: House Republicans sidestep effort to impeach Hegseth
articles.snippet: In a 211 to 204 vote, House Republicans sent proposed impeachment articles against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, quashing the effort.
articles.full_text:
The House voted Tuesday evening to send the proposed impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively quashing an effort to oust Hegseth from his cabinet post.
In a 211 to 204 vote, House Republicans sidestepped an effort proposed by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to impeach Hegseth. Massie charged that Hegseth was negligent and conducted illegal activity in his handling of counternarcotics operations and extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and Pacific; attacking Iran in February without congressional approval; retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for the veteran lawmaker’s statements to troops on illegal orders; capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro without a declaration of war; and other operations.
“Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law,” the articles stated.
The decision to send the articles to the Judiciary Committee likely delays the vote until January, when Democrats take over the majority in Congress.
As of Thursday, Democrats won 256 seats in the House to the Republicans’ 168, while in the Senate, Democrats have at least 54 seats to 44 Republican seats.
If the House votes to impeach Hegseth next year, a two-thirds majority would be needed on any of the articles to force Hegseth out of office.
In a rare news conference Tuesday morning before the vote, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” seeking to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.”
Noting that President Donald Trump was impeached twice but not convicted, Hegseth said he would “take that company every day of the week.”
“These resolutions are a farce. They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders,” Hegseth said.
Trump has said he would stand by his defense secretary, saying Monday that he’s “done a very good job.”
If the effort had succeeded, it would have marked the second impeachment of a U.S. defense secretary and third of a cabinet member. In 2024, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over President Joe Biden’s immigration policies at the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate voted to dismiss the charges before it went to trial.
Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 on corruption charges shortly after he resigned. He was later acquitted in the Senate.
A survey released in October by the military-veterans advocacy non-profit Common Defense found that troops and family members are uncomfortable with what they see as the politicization of the armed forces.
According to the survey, conducted by Change Research, 54% of active-duty personnel surveyed disapproved of Hegseth, while 64% of military family members disapproved.
A majority of the group of 731 active-duty troops, veterans and military family members also believe decisions within the department were being made for political gain, and 53% of active-duty personnel said the politicization was making them want to leave the military sooner than anticipated.
Nearly half the active-duty personnel also said they oppose Operation Epic Fury, the United States’ operation against Iran.

articles.title: US soldier arrested in UK for suspected ‘espionage’ for Russia
articles.snippet: A senior U.S. soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian ​intelligence, British police said on Tuesday.
articles.full_text:
A senior U.S. soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said on Tuesday, after the U.S. removed aircraft from British military bases over a separate apparent threat from Iran.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest of the 41-year-old man was related to “allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, added: “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”
The arrest, which took place near the city of Gloucester, west England, on Tuesday, “is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations,” British police said.
But it occurred the day after the U.S. removed refuelling aircraft from a British airbase in the second such apparent evacuation in three months.
Planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England, on Monday, which, according to the Wall Street Journal, was prompted by a threat from Iran.
The U.S. in September withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford on security grounds over an incident police have linked to Iran, which has denied any links to attacks or incidents in Britain.
The soldier arrested on Tuesday was detained on suspicion of offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Police said the country to which the allegations relate is Russia.

articles.title: Most Americans want new Democratic Congress to end Trump’s Iran war, poll finds
articles.snippet: A new Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran.
articles.full_text:
Majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority U.S. Congress to act to end the war with Iran and to repeal tariffs put in place by President Donald Trump, signaling demand for quick action to address the high cost of living, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The four-day poll, completed on Monday, showed 71% of Americans — including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans — want U.S. Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran that Trump launched alongside U.S. ally Israel in February.
Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives since at least 2008 in last week’s midterm elections, in a sharp rebuke to Trump’s Republicans over high costs and a deeply unpopular war. Democrats will take power when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.
A smaller but still-significant share of respondents — 62% — said they would support an effort to repeal tariffs on imports put in place by the Trump administration.
The war with Iran has pushed fuel prices sharply higher, adding to inflation already stoked by the new taxes Trump slapped on hundreds of imported goods. Trump has defended the war as necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. The tariffs, he has said, will boost American industry by protecting it from cheap imports.
Democratic Party leaders have vowed to address cost of living concerns, and say they will try to force an end to the US war with Iran. Many in the party have also vowed to end Trump’s tariffs.
Desire for bipartisanship
Large majorities of people in both political parties said it was important for Trump to make an effort to work with Democrats and for Democratic leaders in the new Congress to try to work with the president.
Nine in 10 respondents said cost of living issues should be a focus for the Congress during its first 100 days. Smaller shares wanted a focus on issues like artificial intelligence regulation, immigration reform and climate change.
Opposition to impeachment
But many Americans appear concerned Democrats will use their new power to launch legal proceedings against Trump. Some 42% of poll respondents said it would be “bad for the country” if the new Congress tried to impeach Trump, compared with 33% who said it would be good for the country. The rest weren’t sure or didn’t answer the question.
Congressional Democrats are divided on how to bring down healthcare costs, and also disagree on how aggressively to target Trump, including whether to impeach the president or members of his cabinet. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to face a House impeachment vote this week, following a move by a Republican lawmaker.
While Trump said after the elections he would “probably” get along with Democrats, he also promoted Stephen Miller, a polarizing aide who has called the Democratic Party a domestic extremist group, to be his new White House chief of staff.
While the poll showed Trump’s approval rating near the lowest level of his political career, at 32%, it also showed Democrats were not particularly popular either.
Some 45% of Americans had a favorable view of Democrats, while 51% had an unfavorable view. Some 35% had a favorable view of Republicans and 60% viewed them unfavorably.
Asked which party had a better approach to regulating artificial intelligence, which could be an important issue for Congress in the coming months, 28% picked Democrats and 20% picked Republicans while the rest said they weren’t sure or that neither was better.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from 1,705 U.S. adults and had a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

articles.title: Ukraine urges US to speed up interceptor deliveries as Russia targets power grid
articles.snippet: Ukraine's foreign minister urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to accelerate deliveries of interceptors as Russia attempts to break Ukranian morale ahead of its winter months.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine’s foreign minister said he had urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday to accelerate deliveries of interceptors as Russia ramps up attacks on energy infrastructure to break Ukrainian morale during the winter months.
Speaking after talks with Rubio on the sidelines of a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris, Andrii Sybiha told Reuters he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took place in Abu Dhabi.
“We should work on the peace track, but in parallel we should continue to pressure Russia,” he said in an interview.
Sybiha said he had requested additional support for Ukraine’s battered energy grid and more air-defence interceptors, while confirming that U.S. intelligence sharing and military assistance through the Priority Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program remained in place.
“I raised the issue of how we could speed up some supply, how we could find a proper way to maybe front-load something, and how we could try to find additional quantities,” he said.
Not optimistic on Black Sea ceasefire
His remarks come as Kyiv seeks assurances of continued Western military backing while supporting diplomatic efforts to explore limited confidence-building measures with Moscow.
Commenting on the U.S.-mediated talks now underway between Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi, Sybiha said: “Ukraine has serious intentions … We try to use any opportunity to speed up peace efforts and to make peace closer.”
He said Ukraine remained prepared to discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure.
Sybiha said proposals for a Black Sea ceasefire had been conveyed to Russia through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India, but added he was “not so optimistic” about progress and was still awaiting a response from Moscow.
Sybiha says Putin wants to break Ukrainian spirit
Sybiha reiterated Kyiv’s accusations that Russia is deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter.
“[Russian President Vladimir Putin] tries to break our spirit during the winter,” he said.
Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war, now well into its fifth year.
Sybiha was attending a meeting in Paris of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, as well as the European Union.
He said the cost of the war would rise significantly in 2027 and expressed hope that Kyiv could secure longer-term financial commitments from its partners by the end of the year.
“We need macrostability,” he said. “For domestic purposes, it keeps the spirit of our people strong when they understand that at least for one to two years we have long-term commitments.”
Sybiha said his family in Kyiv — including three children — like most Ukrainians, often had only a few hours of electricity a day.
“It means no heating, no water, no sanitation, so it’s a big challenge for us,” he added.

articles.title: First-ever Collaborative Combat Aircraft fly in formation, demonstrate air combat maneuvers
articles.snippet: For the first time, Shield’s Hivemind enabled CCAs to fly in a “multi-ship” formation and execute beyond-visual-range counter-air tactics.
articles.full_text:
For the first time, the U.S. Air Force’s semi-autonomous drones flew in formation and executed air combat maneuvers.
Shield’s Hivemind, the autonomy software that “runs” Collaborative Combat Aircraft flights, helped multiple CCAs fly in a “multi-ship” formation and execute beyond-visual-range counter-air tactics, according to a recent company release.
The release did not specify how many aircraft flew in formation or which CCA participated in the Oct. 26 exercise.
“We are excited that the aircraft and mission systems are reaching a level of integration to start showing what Hivemind can really do,” Todd Wesley, vice president of Hivemind engineering at Shield, said in the announcement.
Each flight generates data that contributes to a software release, per the statement, which supports decisions on testing and fielding.
“The combined Hivemind and aircraft software release process is nearing the point where the Air Force can fly a sortie, update the software overnight and fly again the next day,” Wesley said. “I’m grateful to the Air Force operators, engineers and test teams who fly with us and help us build trust on every flight.”
The demonstration comes as the Air Force announced its intention to have 500 combat-ready, semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet size of 1,000. For the CCA program, the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request included $996.5 million in procurement funding, as well as $150 million in advanced procurement for the following fiscal year and $1.37 billion in continued research and development, for a total program request of $2.37 billion.
The new Shield milestone in the CCA program comes after a F-22 raptor completed airborne tactical command and in-flight control of a YFQ-44A last month, serving as a “quarterback” and giving high-level directives to the Anduril-made CCA.
Meanwhile, Shield AI announced last week its decision to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction to expand the contractor’s drone-warfare capabilities.
The move to absorb Echodyne — which can produce next-generation, solid-state radar systems — was said to support Shield’s expansion into different areas of unmanned systems.

articles.title: The Army’s coming C2 challenge is fighting across thousands of miles
articles.snippet: Breaking down stovepipes, managing data and enabling better decision making are key components of the Army’s NGC2 plan.
articles.full_text:
The Army’s Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) initiative aims to build a unified data infrastructure that can speed up data collection, management, analysis and decision-making not only for its commanders and troops in the field, but also with partners, allies and other branches of the US military.
Breaking Defense spoke with Josh Wallin, Defense Program fellow at the Center for a New American Security, on what needs NGC2 will meet, the data infrastructure necessary to implement NGC2 and how it will help speed up the response to constantly changing threats on the battlefield.
Breaking Defense: What is the threat scenario driving the need for NGC2?
Wallin: There are a few different pieces of this. One is the recognition of just how important the EM spectrum is, how important emissions are and the degree to which we’re seeing jamming and interference and tracking emissions in Ukraine by the Russians.
Another is recognizing the fact that when we’re going against a more capable adversary. In an Indo-Pacific scenario, there’s just a much greater concern about what they can do to mess with communications, mess with data links between forces in the Army specifically.
Another piece is thinking about the distances that you’re dealing with. In the GWOT (Global War on Terror) era, certainly in Iran now or even in Ukraine, we haven’t faced the potential distances we would in the Pacific, and recognizing that you’re trying to connect a bunch of systems that may be located potentially thousands of miles apart from each other.
If we look at how the Army has to operate in the Pacific, it’s not just a distance issue. It’s also a network infrastructure issue.
It’s certainly an infrastructure issue. For at least the last few decades we haven’t really come in direct contact with an adversary that’s going to be targeting the spectrum quite so much. That’s important to be preparing for.
On the infrastructure piece, yes, there is commercial infrastructure that can support things. It’s not that that infrastructure doesn’t necessarily exist at all in the Pacific. I’m not an expert on how all of the Starlink satellites, as an example, have been distributed, but if you had terminals in the Pacific, my presumption is that you would probably still have connectivity in that way. Obviously you’re going to be less able to rely on commercial cellular infrastructure if that’s something you want to be using.
A big component of that is going to also end up being bandwidth. One of the things that the Army is seeing in Ukraine right now is the volume of data, of transmissions that are going out, and especially with all of these distributed operating concepts that the Army, Navy, Air Force are all looking at. There’s a recognition of the fact that you’re going to have to constantly be passing data between a bunch of different nodes to keep them synchronized. So a bunch of different deployed forces, to keep them in sync, you’re going to have less of this concept of centralization or mass in particular locations where it may be much easier to pass information.
What will NGC2 change for the Army at the mission level?
The cross-functional piece that I was alluding to before, to this idea that we should be able to connect systems across different functions with a recognition that data from one – what would have been stovepiped – may be valuable to another one.
There’s a recognition, in Ukraine as an example, that the targeting cycle is very fast. We might be talking on the order of minutes from acquisition to servicing a target. One goal is speeding things up, having that cross functional data that you can take advantage of.
Another piece is even more basic than that when you’re talking within particular functions. For air defense, when we look at systems like Patriot and THAAD, it’s a recent development that those systems are able to talk to and cue each other, that a THAAD radar is able to control a Patriot interceptor.
There is a general recognition of the fact that if we’re going to look at these layered defense concepts, you can’t have stovepiped systems that are acting completely on their own. It’s, one, super inefficient. Two, given the volume of threats we may be facing, it simply may lead to cases in which you can’t match the incoming threat because you’re not able to move information quickly enough and coordinate across units.
We have seen new threats emerging and changing rapidly. How will NGC2 help the Army adapt to that?
NGC2 seems focused on trying to modularize things as much as possible, trying to separate out those hardware pieces. How do we actually have data links? What cable is connected to what radio which is transmitting to which satellite? Separating that from the actual compute infrastructure you need, separating that from the data infrastructure you need.
They’re trying to separate out the software that manages all of your data. An application layer is going to sit on top of that, which is what soldiers are actually tapping into for their particular roles. The idea is if an adversary has adapted a novel way to jam or target or track some of your infrastructure, such as terminals for satellites, you would be able to quickly swap that out for some less vulnerable piece of hardware without having to change all of the things that sit above that.
There are staggering amounts of data being collected. How can that data be managed and used effectively?
The Army is pushing for this centralization of data across functions. Previously we had stovepiped systems where air-defense defense systems may have their own data and communication infrastructure. Logistics might have a separate one. Fires might have a separate one. The idea is that if we can unify all of that data, maybe we can usefully look at correlation across different data sources for different concerns.
If we think about something like logistics, we’re having all these conversations about just-in-time logistics and being able to manage distributed operations. You may want information about ongoing operations and the threat picture. You might want to be connected into intelligence directly. Unifying the data is one piece of that, being able to draw interesting conclusions from how data for different functions might relate to each other.
On the analytical piece, the buzzword continues to be artificial intelligence (AI), the hope that you’ll be able to automatically analyze portions of this data to present it usefully and quickly to operators. A part of that is being able to automate what processes you can, such as using AI or other data analysis techniques to speed up some of the tasks that might be highly manual right now or be able to get a 60 percent solution on something that was 100 percent manual before, and then freeing up more operators’ time.
As NGC2 is built and implemented, how can the Army ensure that it meets not only today’s needs but future needs?
From a hardware perspective, because of the proliferation of larger amounts of compute, there’s a bit more wiggle room in terms of systems being able to do things long term. Because compute is shrinking so much, because it’s becoming more widespread, that gives a nice runway for long-term applications. Maybe compute won’t go as stale quite so quickly for the things that we’re talking about.
The other piece is the Army is very aware and they seem to be really focusing on this idea that they’re not acquiring software solutions or hardware solutions for decades. They’re not expecting that they’re going to be using these same systems 60 years from now. They are really trying to be able to adapt quickly.

articles.title: NATO taps Ukraine as red-team in drills to ‘trigger an adaptation cycle’
articles.snippet: “What we’ve done so far, we took some experience from Ukraine, for example, where we hid some Ukrainian forces and Ukrainian-made USVs, and made them the red team against the blue force of NATO,” Adm. Pierre Vander told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
MILAN — As NATO races to update its battlefield tactics, a senior official said the use of Ukrainian forces as a “red team” in exercises is meant to “trigger an adaptation cycle” within the alliance.
“My job is to build the capabilities of victory. What we’ve done so far, we took some experience from Ukraine, for example, where we hid some Ukrainian forces and Ukrainian-made USVs and made them the red team against the blue force of NATO,” Adm. Pierre Vandier, Supreme Allied Commander of NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT), told Breaking Defense on Monday.
Vandier didn’t point to any specific exercises, but Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has said that in 2025’s REPMUS exercises off Portugal, Kyiv’s “red team” forces defeated NATO members at sea in five out of five combat scenarios, reportedly in part using unmanned surface vessels.
The threat from unmanned surface vessels has not escaped Vandier. In the current security landscape, he said, if a military were to conduct amphibious operations, it would be equally threatened by naval and aerial drones. “So you cannot envisage any kind of operations without counter-drone [defenses]” and must be able to counter incoming swarms of them.
NATO is also preparing for the modern fight through an initiative called Fight Club within its Joint Warfare Centre. Fight Club is part of a larger five-year campaign and is envisioned as a strategic debate forum that brings together external experts and NATO personnel.
Within Fight Club, Vandier said NATO makes “military vignettes,” essentially focused hypothetical scenarios used to test operational concepts and doctrine to “see where the limit is” in a military concept. “To see,” for instance, “how many drones as part of a swarm will submerge a navy, where is the known limit to trigger adaptation,” he said.
Assessing The Russian Naval Posture
Last month, another NATO official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Breaking Defense that the alliance has tracked a significant decline in Russian naval presence in the Mediterranean. Until early September, Moscow observed a two-month naval hiatus in the strategic body of water.
However, as Ukraine heads into its fifth winter at war, Vandier said the Russians have been able to sustain momentum in undersea warfare capabilities.
“If you consider the anti-submarine domain, I think the Russians have kept pace in building some good capabilities, like the Yasen-class [advanced nuclear-powered attack submarines], which are good submarines,” Vandier said.
He added that the anti-submarine warfare domain is one of the “main domains of concern” for the alliance.

articles.title: When networks are contested, paring down the data may mean better logistics at the edge
articles.snippet: AI and software can improve logistics, but only if they work with limited bandwidth.
articles.full_text:
As supply lines and communications networks become priority targets for adversaries, building logistics capabilities that can move personnel and materiel safely and effectively will be critical to military efforts.
Doing so requires building a digital infrastructure that can enable technologies such as software-defined systems, smart warehousing and remote updates, allowing logisticians and troops in the field to work through contested environments to successfully carry out missions.
In a recent webinar, Breaking Defense examined these challenges with Matthew Constanzi, lead for the C5ISR Center’s Sustainment Transformation Predictive Logistics Team at Army DEVCOM; Josh Wallin and Carlton Haelig, fellows at the Defense Program for the Center for a New American Security; and Mike Zizza, sales and growth leader for Wind RiverX.
“The biggest challenge that I’ve seen from my position is the Army’s ability to execute what some will term precision logistics, and that’s just being able to provide the accurate amount of supplies that you need across the battlefield,” said Costanzi, “and doing that in dispersed and communication-denied and degraded environments.
“Within that challenge itself, it really boils down to the ability for the Army to be able to capture accurate and timely tactical-level logistics asset information from both assets and commodities on the battlefield.”
Building the communications and logistics backbones needed to meet that precision logistics challenge requires accurate and timely data, software-driven capabilities and dependable communications networks.
Using data, not drowning in it
Logistics efforts in contested environments start with reliable, usable data. While sensor networks collect vast amounts of data, there is a difference between data and usable data. Without tools to sort through reams of data and make it digestible for those who need to use it, forces run the risk of drowning in information that they can’t effectively make sense of.
“There is a human capital aspect to it,” said Haelig. “By aggregating all of this data, you also present a challenge where folks might raise a question and say, ‘How do we make sense of this? How do we know that this data is accurate? How do we know that it’s the appropriate data for whatever it is we’re trying to get done?’
“And you have to sell it to the actual operators, whether they’re civilians or uniformed operators, that this is going to make their job easier, it is going to make these processes more effective; and you also have to give them the tools to do so.”
Software helps meet this challenge, and artificial intelligence (AI) is already offering ways to help manage data, with those capabilities only expected to grow as AI becomes more effective at sorting through massive datasets to provide usable data. Putting those tools into the hands of both rear-guard logisticians and frontline troops offers the ability to quickly and accurately identify key elements such as open logistics routes, potential areas that may be contested or denied and alternate wayfinding capabilities for both crewed and uncrewed delivery platforms.
Costanzi pointed out that the C5ISR Center is already working on these tools. The center has a proof of concept that it is testing to capture bulk information from fuelers and mobile fuel storage and distribution units, move that data autonomously into command and control (C2) nodes, then push it into the Army data fabric so it can be used by sustainment planners and other warfighting applications. The center is also working with the armaments and soldier Centers to track ammunition from its initial procurement to its consumption rates in the field.
“The big heavy hitters of the Army today are fuel and ammunition, so tracking those and knowing what is at each echelon so that you can provide resupply in a more precision manner definitely is key,” he said.
Quantity of data matters, but quality matters much more, and building tools to help take some of the cognitive burden off of operators will be critical to effective logistics, said Wallin.
“Being able to do things like automatic prediction, making recommendations – even things like filling out supply orders automatically – that’s where we see some potential benefit here,” he said. “Those are things that hopefully can avoid having human operators just being overwhelmed by the amount of information that’s coming in. It’s not just getting more information in, it’s having the tools in place so that operators are actually able to process it.”
Software-driven logistics
The fundamental question of logistics is how to get people and materiel from Point A to Point B safely and efficiently. The answers to that question will vary widely based on region – using highway networks in Europe is a far different logistical challenge than island-hopping in the Pacific – but when logistics are needed in contested environments, the key considerations include identifying usable alternate routes and protecting assets from confiscation or attacks. Being able to use software to help identify and mitigate those challenges speeds up the process and allows for rapid adaptation when necessary.
The Army’s Next-Generation Command and Control (NGC2) effort is driving implementation of software capabilities for logistics. Much of the Army’s logistics efforts still run on paper, but NGC2 aims to build a software structure that will modernize logistics through methods such as digitizing Preventive Maintenance Checks and Services (PCMS), AI-assisted technical manual navigation, troubleshooting, reporting and even capabilities such as medical evacuations.
“All that reporting was done in either spreadsheets or across a couple different enterprise systems, if there even was an enterprise system,” said Costanzi. “They’re trying to pull all that together into basically a sustainment planning tool, planning and execution tool under that NGC2 umbrella.”
Automating these processes not only takes some of the workload off of human operators, but also helps streamline data collection and evaluation. If a logistician has to manually track replacement parts, there is the potential for inaccurate counting, outdated information about stockpiles or data-entry duplication, raising the risk of old or wrong data giving a false picture of materiel on hand. And as assets move around, accurately tracking what assets are where – along with all of their necessary supplements such as replacement parts, fuel and ammunition – is critical to developing a true understanding of supplies on hand, resupply needs and readiness.
“All of that begins with these kinds of uncontested, peacetime software solutions, and from what I understand, these are being exercised in these types of operational environments, and these pitfalls and gaps are being raised as issues,” said Haelig. “But you can’t lose sight of the contested part of the contested logistics problem.”
Software and initiatives such as NGC2 will help solve – or are beginning to solve – some of these challenges, but as Zizza points out, NGC2 will also include legacy systems that are already in the field, and any software solution will have to be functional on the edge to be a truly effective logistics tool.
“The core of that is the idea of software being the real backbone of these systems, and systems of systems that are living code that can be modernized and updated,” said Zizza. “You could argue that contested logistics is ultimately a software resilience problem as much as a physical one, as much as one that’s challenged by weather and extreme distances like in places like the Pacific. When looking at software, being responsive equals survivability, and that equals readiness.”
The importance of reliable communications
Logistics networks run on dependable communications, and in contested environments existing networks may not be easy to access or may not be available at all. In many cases, US forces will be required to bring the network with them or adapt to communications infrastructure such as private 5G networks.
But as logistics tools become increasingly cloud-based, data connectivity increases in importance, and must be maintained to allow forces to communicate and effectively move assets where they need to be. The US and its allies will need to be able to implement communications capability at every level, so that even if they cannot connect to the upper echelon, frontline tactical units will still be able to share information and communicate with each other.
“You need to have really good resilience in your network, and it’s not just resilience in the sense of being able to keep all of your logistics nodes connected at all times, it’s being able to gracefully degrade,” said Wallin. “It’s accepting the fact that when you’re up against a very capable adversary, it is likely that you’re going to lose some nodes. That could be digitally, so it could be you lose communications; it could be physically, meaning you simply don’t have access to certain places because they’re being held under threat.
Costanzi echoed that concern, with the added note that forces in the field will not always have access to the same kinds of communications networks that vendors or planners have available to them as they are designing and testing logistics tools.
“All these vendors are working off of high-speed data connections, and I don’t know that we’re always going to see that in the field,” said Costanzi. “We need to make sure that we have ways to pare our data down smaller to be able to work in those degraded environments, or we’re going to end up fighting blind.”

articles.title: Iran-backed network directed London attacks over FaceTime, US prosecutors say
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: An indictment unsealed Tuesday says the broader campaign, targeting Jewish and American sites, included attacks on synagogues in Belgium, the Netherlands and London, and U.S. bank buildings in Amsterdam and Paris.
articles.full_text:
Iran-backed network directed London attacks over FaceTime, US prosecutors say
The U.S. accused three men of orchestrating attacks across Europe on behalf of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), including a London arson incident that was recorded for propaganda.
An indictment unsealed Tuesday says the broader campaign, targeting Jewish and American sites, included attacks on synagogues in Belgium, the Netherlands and London, and U.S. bank buildings in Amsterdam and Paris. It also included a stabbing in London that left two Jewish men seriously injured.
Prosecutors say the same network later plotted to attack RAF Fairford, a British air base used by U.S. bombers, with vans and what the plotters intended to be explosives. During the attack one suspect directed the vans toward the base by phone from Iran, while another, already jailed in New York, relayed coded instructions through calls with relatives.
The superseding indictment adds two defendants to a case against Mohammad al-Saadi, an alleged commander of the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah who has been jailed in New York since May.
The additional defendants are Mohsen Mohajeri, whom prosecutors identify as an IRGC operative, and Mohammed Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi who once lived in Britain. Both are at large and believed to be in Iran. All three face terrorism charges carrying potential life sentences.
Prosecutors say that recording the attempted attacks for propaganda was an essential part of the network’s operations. The indictment includes images of them directing attacks from a room in Iraq, as well as recordings of instructions given to the attackers.
During an arson attack on a Jewish charity's building in London in April, al-Hassani told the attacker to “light one in your hand,” “light it” and “throw the fourth one,” according to the indictment. The attack was streamed over FaceTime and projected onto a large screen with the militia’s logo. The IRGC operative filmed the proceedings and the men directing it.
Two days earlier, al-Hassani allegedly directed another arson attack on Iran International, a London-based media organization that has repeatedly faced attacks from the Iranian regime.
Again over a video call, al-Hassani told the attacker to get close to the gate and ensure he could see what was happening on camera. During another attack on a London synagogue the following day, he urged the attacker to “light it up like a Christmas tree.”
In March, when al-Saadi asked the IRGC operative Mohajeri about working with his militia on joint attacks involving drones and missiles, Mohajeri agreed and told him to “make sure to photograph a video and pictures.”
The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or HAYI, which prosecutors describe as a front for Kataib Hezbollah and the IRGC. The group claimed about 18 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe between March and April, beginning days after the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran.
HAYI also claimed that drones carrying radioactive material had targeted the Israeli Embassy in London, although police found no hazardous material after investigating the incident. Al-Saadi had received videos days earlier showing men in hazmat suits posing beside a drone that had been fitted with vials of an unspecified white powder.
Hybrid Theory
The new indictment gives the most detailed account yet of how the attacks were directed from afar — drawing on recordings, images and messages exchanged across several apps — and comes amid concerns over what Western authorities describe as “hybrid warfare” and “state-sponsored terrorism.”
Much of the evidence comes from al-Saadi's own iPhone, which FBI agents seized after he was first detained in Turkey in May. Prosecutors say it contained recordings of FaceTime calls, raw attack footage and messages with a Kataib Hezbollah contact.
FaceTime calls are end-to-end encrypted, meaning Apple cannot access their content while the calls are ongoing, however investigators were able to obtain recordings stored on al-Saadi’s seized phone.
The seizure of this evidence comes amid disputes over law enforcement access to encrypted data, particularly in Europe and the United Kingdom.
Apple is currently challenging a reported British demand for access to protected iCloud data, while the European Commission has outlined plans to explore technical options for lawful access to encrypted evidence.
Images in the new indictment show what prosecutors say are Mohajeri and al-Hassani planning attacks while sitting in front of a laptop displaying a map of London, as well as stills from videos of the men directing attacks live.
Earlier images of al-Saadi show him mingling with senior Iranian and militia commanders. These came from his phone and social media accounts, prosecutors said. The FBI linked his WhatsApp, Snapchat, Telegram and X accounts through a single phone number.
Earlier filings say al-Saadi received raw footage of a bombing of a synagogue in Liège, Belgium, through Telegram and used the app to send footage of an arson attack on Jewish volunteer ambulances in London to a contact saved in his phone as a China-based media company.
Prosecutors also say al-Saadi paid an undercover officer about $3,000 in cryptocurrency in April, which was related to a planned attack on a Manhattan synagogue. The nature of the transaction was not detailed, and no attack took place.
In August, al-Hassani allegedly paid someone to film the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase, which houses U.S. military aircraft and personnel. The following month, paid associates bought vans, barrels of fuel and metal objects that could serve as shrapnel, and researched buying chemicals, according to the indictment.
During the alleged attempted attack towards the end of that month, al-Hassani was described as being in frequent contact by phone with the drivers of three vans heading toward the base, directing their movements from Iran, prosecutors say. It is not clear whether he used normal voice calls or communicated via an app.
At least two of the vans were turned back at a security roadblock. British authorities recovered the vehicles in the early hours of the next morning and arrested their occupants. Police said at the time they found no explosives but seized petrol. Seven people were arrested and released on bail.
Apple, Snap, X and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Al-Saadi's X account, which the FBI says had posted calls for revenge against Americans as early as 2020, remained online Wednesday.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Poland shuts down government services platform ePUAP following cyberattack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The attack targeted a nationwide system that allows users to submit official documents, communicate with government agencies and complete administrative procedures online.
articles.full_text:
Poland shuts down government services platform ePUAP following cyberattack
Poland temporarily shut down a government platform used by citizens and businesses to access public services after detecting and stopping a cyberattack, officials said Tuesday.
The attack targeted ePUAP, a nationwide system that allows users to submit official documents, communicate with government agencies and complete administrative procedures online.
Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said security teams responded immediately to the incident and were working to restore the platform's full functionality.
"The cyberattack on the state ePUAP system was detected and stopped," Gawkowski said in a social media post.
The minister said the infrastructure of Poland's Central Information Technology Center, the government agency responsible for maintaining key digital services, including ePUAP, remained secure.
Officials said the ePUAP platform was taken offline as a precaution rather than because of damage caused by the attack.
"It's not that the system was somehow compromised or its operation was disrupted by this attack," Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told Polish news agency PAP. "We simply disabled it as a precautionary measure."
Authorities have not disclosed how the attack was carried out or who was responsible. There has been no public confirmation that hackers gained access to government systems or stole sensitive information.
The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring the platform, saying services will resume once security specialists complete their work.
According to a notice on the government's website, ePUAP electronic mailboxes remain unavailable to citizens and public institutions. The disruption could also temporarily affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which allows people to access public services and electronically sign official documents.
Poland has faced repeated cyberattacks targeting government institutions, critical infrastructure and private companies in recent months.
In October, Polish online invoicing provider Fakturownia reported a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners.
In September, hackers also stole data from Qbusoft, a Polish healthcare software provider, following a separate breach involving medical technology company MyDr. Polish authorities said the MyDr incident potentially affected information relating to about 19 million people and roughly 12,000 healthcare organizations.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Britain, France set out first guidelines for commercial hacking firms
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The guidelines call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses.
articles.full_text:
Britain, France set out first guidelines for commercial hacking firms
Fourteen governments participating in the Pall Mall Process, a diplomatic effort led by Britain and France to rein in the global spyware industry, adopted their first guidelines for commercial hacking businesses on Wednesday.
The French Foreign Ministry said the guidelines, aimed at addressing abuses associated with the proliferation of commercial cyber intrusion capabilities (CCICs), set out “the first global standard of responsible conduct.”
“Access to certain capabilities once reserved for a handful of specialized government agencies has gradually widened: any actor can now buy ‘off the shelf’ the ability to silently penetrate a phone,” the ministry said.
While it acknowledged those tools have been used in intelligence operations and to tackle organized crime, the ministry warned they “have also been implicated in surveillance campaigns targeting journalists, political officials, activists or businesses.”
The guidelines are non-binding and endorsed by governments rather than industry organizations. They call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses.
Companies should halt sales and support when serious misuse is a credible risk, according to the text, and are asked to “consider” remedies for victims of human rights abuses. There are no penalties for non-compliance and enforcement pressure is expected to come from governments which buy the tools and license their export.
The point of the industry guidelines is “to disincentivise irresponsible activity across the market for CCICs; improve transparency for regulators, vendors and customers; and provide clarity for businesses operating both within and peripherally to the industry,” said the British Foreign Office.
The guidelines were endorsed at the Pall Mall initiative’s third conference, attended by representatives from 43 countries. Fewer than half signed up to endorse them, with signatories including the United Kingdom and France, alongside the United States, Germany, Italy and Japan.
The guidelines “are voluntary in nature,” the ministry said. “They do not create new international legal obligations and do not call into question uses that states consider legitimate in the fields of national security, defense, the fight against organized crime or cybersecurity.
“A voluntary code is not, however, an optional code: one’s word, given before one’s peers, one’s industries and one’s citizens, is a commitment.”
The Pall Mall Process has faced persistent challenges since its launch in London in 2024. While that event drew large technology and cybersecurity firms, it did not feature the controversial businesses whose products had been linked to abuses.
A year later, participants raised concerns that the initiative lacks the ability to actually change how these tools are traded and used. Some noted that Britain and France were seeking to restrict other states’ access to these tools while championing their own spyware industries.
Last year’s conference produced the first code of practice for governments, but no agreement on how to influence company behavior. Twenty-seven countries have since signed the code. It is not clear why the remaining 15 did not endorse the new code on Wednesday.
The ministry said participants would continue their work as “artificial intelligence, the growing automation of certain functions and the emergence of new business models” raise new questions for governments and companies.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: US Army member arrested in UK over allegations of spying for Russia
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The unnamed soldier was arrested by British counterterrorism police “working closely” with U.S. authorities, including the FBI and the military, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
articles.full_text:
US Army member arrested in UK over allegations of spying for Russia
A 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British authorities announced Tuesday.
The unnamed soldier was arrested by U.K. counterterrorism police “working closely” with U.S. authorities, including the FBI and the military, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement. The man is in custody at a London police station.
“While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message—this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement issued by the British counter-terror police.
The man was arrested under sections of the U.K.’s National Security Act that cover espionage. The arrest occurred near Gloucester, a city about 100 miles west of London that is close to the home of GCHQ, Britain’s intelligence, security and cybersecurity agency.
“As part of the investigation officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire,” according to police. “The country to which the allegations relate is Russia.”
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the head U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement that the “senior soldier” who was arrested was “entrusted with sensitive information.”
Earlier this year, Britain’s spy chief warned that Russia is engaged in “daily hybrid activity” against the U.S. and its Western allies.
GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler accused Moscow of “relentlessly targeting critical infrastructure, democratic processes, supply chains and public trust” and that it attacks “from the seabed to cyberspace.”
The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

articles.title: Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday surpasses 1,000 bugs for second month in a row
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: An exploited Outlook vulnerability drew most of the attention in Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday, which listed 1,093 bugs total.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday surpasses 1,000 bugs for second month in a row
More than 1,000 vulnerabilities were disclosed by Microsoft in the latest Patch Tuesday release as federal cybersecurity officials ordered civilian agencies to patch exploited bugs from Google, Barracuda and Cisco.
Among the 1,093 bugs disclosed on Tuesday, Microsoft said one is being exploited in the wild: CVE-2026-124194. The company said it has a severity score of 6.5 and impacts Microsoft Outlook.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies until the end of the month to patch it.
Microsoft said the bug was discovered by Benoît Sevens using Anthropic’s Claude, writing that an attacker “could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook.”
“Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user,” the company said.
Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, said an attack using the vulnerability may allow someone to sign in as the exploited user.
Several experts said CVE-2026-124194 was the only exploited bug outlined in Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday release but there were 63 vulnerabilities rated critical. Narang noted that Tuesday’s release brings Microsoft to more than 5,160 vulnerabilities disclosed this year, which would far surpass any previous year.
Last month, more than 1,400 vulnerabilities were disclosed by Microsoft after about 900 in September.
In addition to Microsoft’s disclosures, Google, Cisco, Adobe, Barracuda, Ivanti and several other companies released patches for dozens of bugs, several of which were spotlighted by CISA as being exploited.
CISA gave federal agencies until Friday to patch CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 — two bugs affecting Barracuda's email security product. They also ordered all federal agencies to investigate potential compromises related to both vulnerabilities.
Response to N-able vulnerabilities
A researcher also uncovered more than 30 serious vulnerabilities in N-Central, a popular remote management tool that IT teams use to monitor and run networks remotely.
The company behind it, N-able, took all hosted N-central environments offline and ordered customers to turn off their servers.
“As expected, we are observing scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code. At this time, we have no evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited,” the company said on Tuesday.
“During this time, customers will be unable to access their Hosted N-central classic environment, and associated services may be unavailable.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.
Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.
The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.
IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.
Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.
The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.
Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.
A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.
That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.
More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.
Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.snippet: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.
This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.
According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.
Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.
“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”
Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.
Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.
Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”
Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.
Thank you as always. Your concern and actions for others is very much appreciated by all, including those not aware of it.
With respect, John Royal
I wonder whether a goal of a bug-free Windows is mathematically possible, or whether there will always be residual “bugs” in the form of some marginal configurations and conditions that can never be made fully fault-safe.
I’m sure it’s possible to have bug-free software, but I’ve never seen it in anything but very simple programs. There are ALWAYS bugs. (I worked in software QA/testing for 20 years…)
Excellent reporting, as usual. Thank you BK.

Microsoft says the November 2026 cumulative updates resolve USB audio issues plaguing Windows users who have installed security updates released since September.
The company explained, when it acknowledged this known issue days after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday, that USB Audio Class 1.0 devices failed to start or produce audio on some systems after installing recent updates.
Some affected users reported seeing no audio output, unresponsive volume controls and sound settings, and "This device cannot start (Code 10)." errors in Device Manager, while others said the impacted USB audio speakers fail only when using multichannel audio features, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes.
These audio issues affect both server (Windows Server 2012 and later) and client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) systems.
Microsoft released out-of-band updates on September 14 to fix the symptoms experienced on devices using 8-channel or 3D audio modes and has now addressed the remaining issues in security updates released as part of this month's Patch Tuesday.
"The symptoms are resolved in the Windows security update released on November 10, 2026 (KB5132061) and later updates," Microsoft said in a Windows release health dashboard update.
"We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one."
While Microsoft has yet to provide an official workaround for those who can't immediately install the November 2026 security updates, some users have restored audio on affected Windows PCs by switching to 2-channel mode.
Previous audio issues affecting Windows systems
Two years ago, Microsoft also confirmed an issue that caused game audio to unexpectedly increase to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems and blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on systems with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers due to blue screen of death (BSOD) issues.
In January 2025, Microsoft addressed a similar issue triggered by the KB5050094 optional preview cumulative update, which caused audio playback issues and Code 10 errors on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers.
More recently, in September 2025, it lifted a safeguard hold preventing Windows 11 24H2 upgrades on systems with Dirac audio improvement software because compatibility issues caused Bluetooth speakers and headsets to malfunction.
With the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft also resolved Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems triggered by the October 2026 Windows Server security updates.
